text:
Thread: Is it just me or have races gotten worse?
Comment: Race producer checking in, 35 years experience at a not-for-profit. Also have raced over 500 races lifetime so lots of experience from the runner's side of the fence too.The cost of race production is up a ton the last decade. I would say it started a little before covid. Many of the things that are up the most are fixed costs - for example for our biggest race city permits were under $4k a decade ago, now over $10k. Police and EMT services have gone from ~$35-$40/hour to ~$90/hour. No matter if we have 1500 runners or 5000 runners we still need the same number of police and EMTs out on the course. The cost for the announcer's PA system over doubled. Tent costs close to double. Those are all big ticket items that have major impact on the financials.The cost of "consumables", like shirts and medals, is honestly not up that much. A decade ago we were in the $7-$8 range per runner, now it's $10-$12 for the same items. Things like portos, insurance, music licenses, Gatorade, cups are all variable costs - they're all up but can be managed depending on how many runners we expect.In many cases sponsorship dollars and in-kind donations have fallen. That part of the game has always been a challenge so not really anything new. Coming out of covid we lost significant silver tier cash sponsors. Our top sponsors have had our back all the way through, been incredibly supportive and that means the world to us. But the silver, bronze, and supporter categories we see a lot of tire kickers but not a lot of activation. When those drop we look to the entrants to make up the difference.Another thing we're trying to do that costs money is reward our volunteers. We had a lot of discussions with our universe during covid, and one thing that kept coming up is "you really could do more for your volunteers". Because of that we now stipend some volunteer groups, non-profits who work our aid stations or other areas where we use bulk volunteers. We're providing goodie bags for volunteers who are out on the course for hours keeping the runners on track. We're inviting our top level volunteer coordinators to join us for the catered post-race meal and providing them with a higher quality race shirt/jacket/hat. Any things we can do to retain volunteers is a must-do at this stage.One factor, and this has ALWAYS been a weird one to me, is that low cost races for some reason do not tend to get runner support. So a lot of times we will price a race in the range of what the market is charging rather than basing the entry fees on what it actually costs to produce the race. Example - we started up a half marathon 20 years ago. It was a no frills race - just an accurate course, water on the course (no gels no sports drink), light post-race food, no medal, no shirt. Point to point so you got a bus to the start. Portos of course. Entry fee was $15. We got a couple hundred runners. Good time of the year, not much competition, good weather. After year 3 we surveyed local runners to ask them why they weren't doing this race. Heard from a lot of runners something along the lines of "I don't expect a good half marathon to cost $15, so I think it's probably not a good race." Year 4 we bumped the entry fee up to $35, a little below the local market, didn't add any extras. Entries shot up to 500. Year 5, same price, we sold out 600 slots in 3 days and added a 2nd wave of 400 that we also sold out. Since then we've kept it as a market rate race. We have added some perks over the years like finisher medals and a nice post-race with food & beer, and we now draw 1500+. Consumer behavior has always been SO WEIRD to me!!!Happy to answer any questions anyone has about what we see from the race producer side of the game.

Thread: Started running at 39. For those who also started later — what happened to your fitness in years 2–4?
Comment: I started running at 39 during Covid when I found myself with too much time on my hands. I was running maybe 2-3 miles a day a couple times a week. I have never been a fit person - always the fat girl with a big personality who couldn't even run 60 seconds when I first started. I signed up for my first half on a whim, and ran that in 2021. Ran a few more halfs between '22 and '24.In 2024, I entered the NYC lottery on a whim, saying "there's no way I could run a full marathon, but nobody ever actually gets a spot for the lottery so it's fiiiiine." And that's how I ended up training for and running the 2024 NYC marathon. I crossed the finish line, burst into tears, and said "I'll never do that again." Two weeks later, I signed up for my second full marathon. Today I'm training for #3, with #4/5/6 in the pipeline. I went from running maybe 5-10 miles a week to averaging about 20-25 in the summer, and then 40ish when I'm actually training for something.I've gotten faster, but honestly, I'll always be a back of the pack runner. I'm fine with that. I hope to take about an hour off my marathon time this year (again, I'm very slow, so I have an hour to shave off and still be in the back of the pack). I've lost about 70 lbs and my body is unrecognizable from 2019 me. Literally - I've run into people I haven't seen in years and they didn't recognize me. I'm the healthiest I've ever been, and I can do and enjoy things in ways I wasn't able to before. It's also been a fascinating process as I'm hitting middle age, to watch as I'm getting stronger and fitter and a lot of my peers are moving in the opposite direction. I volunteer for stuff at my daughter's school, and I am being relegated to more physical jobs because so many of the other parents my age physically can't do them. It's wild as a newly-fit person to be in this position. That's been worth it all to me - knowing that I'm getting healthier and stronger to be around longer for my family (hopefully) and to actually ENJOY that time together, not just be a bump on the couch. That's all worth it.

text:
Thread: Is it just me or have races gotten worse?
Comment: Hey! Hoping I can chime in here and provide some insight from a timer’s perspective.Now keep in mind, I’m usually sitting between the runner and the race director, so I’m not directly involved with the permitting and all these other things. Usually the client handles all that.But my understanding is that cities, municipalities, whoever, have been more aggressive in not only what they’re charging for permits for events, but also their requirements to secure those permits.I do a lot of timing throughout Florida and a couple other states, and I can say that in a lot of areas, the race directors I work with are being told that if they want a permit, they have to hire so many police officers per intersection or per number of runners. And those police officers come with an additional off-duty cost. Usually they’re getting paid overtime, and I think that can easily exceed $40 an hour. Same applies to EMTs.So if you’re having, let’s say, 10 police officers and an event is four hours from start to finish for a 10K, we’re talking about $1,600 just for the police officers to be out there. And then you have your permitting fees and everything else.We also have to look at the cost of porta potties, swag, nutrition, marketing, advertising and everything else that goes into it. And on the timer side, those chips that are worn on the back of your bibs also go up in cost over time.So there are so many hidden costs that the runner normally doesn’t see directly that are driving the inflation on these events.And keep in mind, some of these race directors are doing this voluntarily. Some are doing it for a good nonprofit cause. And for some of them, it’s their full-time job. So at the end of the day, they also have to get some sort of return from the event to justify all the time and energy they put in.And I can tell you, for even halfway decent events, those race directors are putting a lot of energy and sweat into making them happen.I hope that helps, and feel free to ask me anything!

Thread: Is it worth doing a Major Marathon?
Comment: If you're any way competitive and looking for a fast time, they're not really the best, until you run fast enough to qualify for some "sub-elite" treatment. The logistics of having so many participants means you'll spend longer on your feet the day before than you'd like, you'll have to drop off your bag and enter the corrals earlier than you'd like and probably won't have room to do any sort of warmup(not that much is needed until you're getting down to sub 2:30ish).But what you are getting is the atmosphere, opportunity to see these cities in a unique way and a sense of achievement. There's nothing like the buzz in a city on marathon day, roads closed to traffic and the energy of the other runners. Once you're realistic about what to expect from the day, you won't be disappointed about not hitting your time goal. Now you might still hit it, but there are just more risks than with a more low key race.

Thread: Is it worth doing a Major Marathon?
Comment: I've never done NY. Could see it being similar.For me, Boston was always THE marathon, with the time entry gating being a big part of it. If you make it to Boston, it means you're good!The excitement builds all morning long. First getting to the buses, then finally boarding. I had a good bus buddy on the journey out to Hopkinton. Then hanging out in Athletes' Village for a while was like being in the world's largest sub-elite warm-up area. Everyone is so happy and excited and stressed. There's a million different approaches to get ready all going on at the same time. Then the march from Athletes' Village to the start line builds it up even more. That first year you don't really know what to expect, but it's not a short distance, and each step is just building anticipation.My first year, my bib was in the 2000s, but on race day I wasn't quite as fit as I was in my qualifying race, so I went to the back of my corral. When you finally start, it's like a stampede. Never before in a race did I feel like I had to keep pace to avoid being run over (in a fun way). From that first mile I felt, "I'm with my people." I did a lot of reflecting on the history of the race and just thinking along the lines of, "this is the race you've heard about since you were a kid." And of course there's a great crowd.Thankfully I was being conservative, so when I hit the Newton Hills, my first thought was actually "these aren't as bad as I expected" (unfortunately in subsequent years they kicked my ass). When I finally summited Heartbreak Hill, I actually teared up a little realizing I had just conquered perhaps the most notorious challenge in road racing, and at that point I knew I had a real shot of going sub-3, which I did not expect to do that day. My plan going into the race was to run hard, but make sure to enjoy myself, but at that point I wanted more, so I left it all out there (it's pretty downhill from that point). Of course, finishing on Boylston Street is just crazy energy. It was made even better by having my family there watching and finding them in the crowd.I always planned to qualify for Boston, run it once, then move on from marathons. Instead, during the course, all I could think was, "I have to do this again." I made it right at 2:59, which was good enough to get me back in the next year. I've run it 4 times now. Each time successively harder. The 4th time really kicked my ass and I missed out on qualifying for 2026. But I'll be back for round 5 in 2027.Hopefully this was helpful. It was fun for me to type this out and relive the memories.I'll add that the front end of the crowd in Chicago is similarly fast to the start of Boston these days, but the Chicago course is wider, so you aren't jammed in together the same way. I love Chicago. It's my local and first marathon. It's just not Boston though.

text:
Thread: Is it just me or have races gotten worse?
Comment: As a volunteer and planner on smaller races, frilly things or add-ons critically depend on volunteer support and engagement. Finding volunteer support and engagement can be extremely difficult. You may wonder, well why does volunteer support matter on whether the race gives out Gus at $1/piece at Mile 7, it's just a box, and money-money right? Well, here's the thing.The most important thing for an RD is actually having a safe, timed race, if there's even a race at all. So permits, traffic control, timing, PA, barricades, toilet, equipment rentals, and general scrounging, etc., all take top priority. Frilly things and add-ons like a free post-race teppanyaki grill feast (wouldn't that be amazing) have to come last, and often, all of those extras depend on a run that is at or near full capacity. Races that depend on walk-ons and walk-ups really can't make safe projections to know, for sure, that the teppanyaki grill can happen.Long story short, if you either want to know the real why, or to help solve the problem, it has to come from volunteering vigorously for local races, and supporting races you're in by registering early and spreading the word to try to get to full capacity.This has nothing to do with margins save a few commercial marathon groups (like RNR of course). Very few people are planning a race to make a $1k sweet profit on a local half or 10k. I'm sure it happens, but if people are expecting free backrubs at those, that's probably a product of unrealistic expectations.
